opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important question, and I'd frame it a little differently than "excitement versus infrastructure." The excitement is what's driving the investment in the first place, and that's not a bad thing. The question is whether we're investing in the right kinds of things, and whether we're being realistic about the timescales.

From where I sit, working mostly on robotics and embodied learning, one thing that's become very clear is that progress in AI is fundamentally tied to scale: scale of data, scale of compute, scale of deployment. Building large-scale compute infrastructure isn't a side issue; it's central. But I'd add that "infrastructure" means more than data centers and chips. For robotics in particular, it means physical hardware that's cheap and reliable enough to deploy widely, and the systems that let those robots collect experience in the real world. That's a very different kind of investment than just buying more GPUs, and I think it's underappreciated.

There's also a temptation to treat this as a race where you pour everything into the most visible thing, the biggest language model or the biggest cluster. I think a healthier approach is a portfolio: invest heavily in compute because we know scaling works, but also in the less glamorous parts like energy, manufacturing capacity, sensors, actuators, and the data pipelines that let systems learn from interacting with the world. Those tend to be the real bottlenecks once the algorithms mature.

And I'd say we should be a bit humble about predictions. The excitement is justified in the sense that the capabilities are real and growing quickly. But the path from a capability demonstrated in the lab to something that changes how people actually live involves a lot of engineering, iteration, and physical buildout. If society treats that buildout as part of the AI project rather than an afterthought, I think we'll end up in a much better place, both in getting the benefits sooner and in being able to deploy these systems responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response warns that concentrating investment on highly visible AI efforts, such as the biggest language model or compute cluster, can crowd out other needed investments, and recommends funding less glamorous bottlenecks as well.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting question, and I think it's worth separating a couple of things. There's the excitement around what AI can do right now, which is mostly in the digital domain, right? Language models, things that process text and images, things that live inside a computer. And then there's the question of what it takes to actually get this stuff out into the physical world, which is where I spend most of my time thinking, because that's where robotics is.

And the thing that I think is sometimes underappreciated is that for the digital stuff, the infrastructure investment is pretty straightforward to reason about. You need compute, you need data centers, you need energy, and those are big investments, but the path from investment to capability is relatively clear. You build more compute, you train bigger models, you get better results. For the physical world, it's much murkier. The bottleneck isn't just compute. It's data. It's actually having robots out there collecting experience, interacting with the world, and that's a kind of infrastructure that we don't really have yet in any meaningful quantity.

So if I were thinking about how society should balance this, I'd say the excitement is probably justified, but it should be directed in a slightly different way than it currently is. Right now a lot of the capital is flowing toward scaling up the same recipe that worked for language models. And that's fine, that will keep producing gains. But I think the really transformative applications, the ones that affect the economy in a deep way, are the ones where AI systems can actually do physical work. And for that, the infrastructure question is not about GPUs, it's about deploying systems in the real world, getting them to a point where they're useful enough to be out there, and then letting that flywheel of data and improvement spin up.

There's also a sense in which I think we should be a little careful about the framing of "balancing" excitement with investment, because historically those things have actually gone together. The excitement is what drives the investment. The risk is more that the excitement gets attached to the wrong timelines or the wrong expectations. If people expect that the physical world is going to be transformed in two years the way the digital world was, they'll be disappointed, and then you get a correction, and that correction can set the field back. So I'd say be excited, invest heavily, but understand that for the embodied stuff, this is going to be a longer road, and the infrastructure that matters most is the stuff that lets us learn from real-world experience at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says much of the capital is flowing toward scaling language models, while physical AI needs investment in robot deployment and real-world data infrastructure, indicating attention can be drawn away from other necessary investments.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be excited, but we should distinguish between making progress in AI and turning that progress into something that improves people’s lives. Those are connected, but they’re not the same thing. If you have a system that can design a better bridge, you still need to build the bridge. You need materials, manufacturing capacity, and people who can actually carry out that work.

Robotics is interesting here because it could help close that gap. But even if the intelligence becomes very capable, deploying robots still requires producing hardware, supplying energy, and figuring out how these systems fit into real environments. Software can spread very quickly. Physical systems take time.

So I wouldn’t frame this as choosing between AI and infrastructure. They’re complementary investments. We should pursue the capabilities while also building the capacity to use them. Otherwise, we could end up with extraordinarily powerful tools whose benefits are constrained by fairly mundane physical bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: The response says AI capabilities and infrastructure are complementary investments, but it does not say that excitement about AI progress can divert attention from other necessary investments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the excitement is useful if it translates into investment in things that let us make progress. AI can sound like a purely software endeavor, but it depends on very physical things: chips, power, data centers, and, if we want these systems to act in the world, robots.

The challenge is that infrastructure takes a long time to build, while our expectations about AI can change very quickly. So I would favor investments that remain useful across a range of outcomes. Better power infrastructure, more capable manufacturing, and access to computing for researchers have value even if a particular prediction about AI turns out to be wrong.

And we should keep investing in research alongside that. More hardware gives us the ability to run bigger experiments, but we still need to figure out which experiments are worth running.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investing in infrastructure and research alongside AI progress, but it does not say that excitement about AI can divert attention from other necessary investments.
